169.title: Pauri 4, sound: saachaa saahib
169.hook: saachaa saahib saach naae bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar
169.howItsDone: The fourth pauri of Japji is recited each morning; its line on the amrit vela is the scriptural root of the Sikh practice of rising before dawn for simran.

segments.voice: Yesterday, veparvaahu, the carefree Giver. Your line was the giver never tires.

Back in camp three came an alarm set five minutes early for the amrit vela, the nectar hour before dawn. That hour came from somewhere specific: this pauri, the fourth step of Japji. Before the early hours, though, hear how it begins. Its first line has a sound you already know: sach, the true, from aad sach, turns up twice, in two different forms, like one word trying on two coats.
screen: `THE ALARM FIVE MINUTES EARLY.` → `IT CAME FROM THIS PAURI.` → `ONE WORD IN TWO COATS.`

segments.voice: The opening line: saachaa saahib, saach naae, bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar. Saachaa: SAA-chaa, the true one. Saahib: SAA-hib, Master, Lord; the same sahib you hear in Japji Sahib and Guru Granth Sahib, a word of honor. Saach: the true again, this time about a name. Naae: NAA-ay, name. Bhaakhiaa: BHAA-khi-aa, spoken, expressed. Bhaau: rhymes with how, with a breath on the b; it means love. Apaar: a-PAAR, without limit, boundless. So the outline is already there: true Master, true name, spoken with boundless love. Now the sound. Saachaa, saahib, saach: the line opens with three s-sounds in a row, soft and steady, like someone walking up to a door. Then bhaakhiaa bhaau, two bh sounds side by side, and the wide, open vowel of apaar. From a narrow door into a very big room. Soon the pauri turns to questions: what can we offer, what words can we say? Then a line you've heard before: amrit vela sach naau vadiaaee veechaar, the early hours, the true name, reflecting on its greatness. Then a word that opens tomorrow: nadar. For now, this first line is almost a whole prayer in miniature: who the One is, what the Name is, and how it's spoken, with love and no limit.
screen: `SAACHAA SAAHIB — TRUE MASTER.` · `SAACH NAAE — TRUE NAME.` · `BHAAU APAAR — BOUNDLESS LOVE.` · `THE AMRIT VELA LINE.` · then, large: `PAURI FOUR.`

segments.voice: Speak the first line softly: saachaa saahib, saach naae, bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar. Twice more, slower, the s-sounds soft and the last word open wide, then almost whispered. Then sit, notice how your breath lengthened on apaar, and let it stay long; if you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

170.title: Pauri 4, meaning: the early hours
170.hook: what can we offer to see His court? In the ambrosial hours, reflect on the true Name; grace opens the door (Japji 4)
170.howItsDone: Following Japji's fourth pauri, many Sikhs rise in the amrit vela before dawn for simran and Nitnem; nadar, the gracious glance, is spoken of throughout Sikh teaching as what finally opens the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, apaar, boundless. Your line was saachaa saahib: true Master, true name, boundless love.

What do you bring when you visit someone important? Flowers for a hostess. A bottle of something for the boss. A card and a cake for a new neighbor. You stand at the door with something in your hands, hoping it's enough. Guru Nanak's fourth pauri stands at a much bigger door, the court of the true Master, and asks exactly that question: what could anyone possibly bring?
screen: `FLOWERS FOR THE HOSTESS.` → `STANDING AT THE DOOR.` → `WHAT COULD ANYONE BRING?`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. True is the Master, true His name, spoken with boundless love. People ask and beg, give, give, and the Giver gives. Then the questions. What can we place before Him, so that His court comes into view? What words can we speak, so that hearing them He would love us? The answer, the one camp three built a practice on: in the amrit vela, the ambrosial hours, reflect on the true Name and its greatness. Not flowers. Not a bottle. Attention, in the quiet before dawn. Then a line people have argued over lovingly for centuries: karmee aavai kaparaa, nadree mokh duaar. Kaparaa is cloth, a garment. Many read it as the body, the robe of this life, which comes by our karma, our actions. Others read karam in its Persian sense, kindness or grace, so even the robe of honor comes by grace. Either way, the second half is the same: nadree mokh duaar. By His nadar, the door of liberation. Nadar is a glance, a gaze, the look someone gives you when they're glad you came; it's the Persian nazar. In Sikh teaching it's the gracious glance of the One, and the pauri says that's what finally opens the door. So the order is lovely. You show up early. You bring attention, not payment. And the door is opened from the other side. The pauri ends: Nanak, know this; the One is all, and true.
screen: `WHAT CAN WE BRING TO THE COURT?` · `ATTENTION, BEFORE DAWN.` · `KARAM — ACTION, OR GRACE?` · `NADAR — THE GRACIOUS GLANCE.` · then, large: `THE DOOR OPENS FROM INSIDE.`

segments.voice: The pauri points to the hours before dawn, and to bringing nothing: no requests, no list, no clever words, just your attention, set down like an empty cup. If you pray, hold the true Name, Waheguru, and wait; if you don't, simply sit at the door and be awake.
Nadar. The gracious glance. In Japji's fourth pauri, by nadar comes the door of liberation.
Your line: the early hour opens. You can't buy the glance, but you can be awake when it comes. That's day one hundred seventy.

171.title: Pauri 5, sound: thaapiaa na jaae
171.hook: thaapiaa na jaae keetaa na hoe
171.howItsDone: The fifth pauri of Japji is recited each morning; its refrain, guraa ik dehi bujhaaee, about the one understanding the Guru gives, comes back at the end of the sixth pauri.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nadar, the gracious glance that opens the door. Your line was the early hour opens.

People make things and set them in place all the time: a trophy in a cabinet, a photo on a shelf, a sign over a shop door. Made, put in place, and there they stay. Today a new stretch of Japji begins, pauris five to eight, and the fifth pauri opens by saying, twice, that the One can't be handled that way. It says it in a line built from two short no's, with a soft, rolling sound.
screen: `A TROPHY SET IN PLACE.` → `A NEW STRETCH: PAURIS 5 TO 8.` → `TWO SHORT NO'S.`

segments.voice: The opening line: thaapiaa na jaae, keetaa na hoe. Thaapiaa: THAA-pi-aa. The th isn't the English th in thin; it's a t with a puff of breath after it, like the t in top said firmly. Thaap means to set up, to install, to establish, the way an image is set on a pedestal. Na jaae: na, not; JAA-ay, can be. Keetaa: KEE-taa, made. Na hoe: na, not; HO-ay, is, becomes. Cannot be installed, cannot be made: two no's, balanced on either side of the line like the two pans of a scale. Then the next line: aape aap niranjan soe. AA-pay aap: himself, by himself. Ni-RUN-jun: stainless, unstained. He is Himself, by Himself, the stainless one. Hear the rhythm: short phrases, each ending on a soft vowel, jaae, hoe, soe. It rocks gently, back and forth. Later in this pauri comes a refrain you'll hear again in the next one: guraa ik dehi bujhaaee. Guraa: Guru. Ik: one. Dehi bujhaaee: give understanding. It's read two ways: as a request, O Guru, give me this one understanding, or as thanks, the Guru has given this one understanding. What that understanding is, tomorrow. So the pauri starts with two no's about what the One is not, and ends with a yes: one understanding, given by the Guru.
screen: `THAAP — TO SET UP, TO INSTALL.` · `TWO NO'S, LIKE A SCALE.` · `AAPE AAP NIRANJAN SOE.` · `GURAA IK DEHI BUJHAAEE.` · then, large: `PAURI FIVE.`

segments.voice: Say it slowly, out loud if you can, with a light puff of breath on the th: thaapiaa na jaae, keetaa na hoe. Add the next line, aape aap niranjan soe, and say all of it once more, softly, feeling it rock back and forth. Then sit in the quiet; if you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

172.title: Pauri 5, meaning: one Giver
172.hook: He cannot be installed or made; the Guru has given one understanding, that there is one Giver of all, never to be forgotten (Japji 5)
172.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the fifth pauri each morning; its refrain, that there is one Giver of all beings who should never be forgotten, is also sung as kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, niranjan, the stainless one, and the sound of pauri five. Your line was thaapiaa na jaae.

Have you ever forgotten who gave you something? A sweater you've worn for years, and one day you realize you have no idea where it came from. A habit picked up from a teacher whose name is gone. People forget givers all the time, not out of ingratitude, just because the gift becomes part of them. The fifth pauri ends with Nanak asking for one thing only: not to forget the Giver.
screen: `A SWEATER, BUT FROM WHOM?` → `THE GIFT BECOMES PART OF YOU.` → `DON'T FORGET THE GIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. He cannot be installed or made; He is Himself, by Himself, the stainless one. Those who serve Him receive honor. Nanak, sing of the treasure of virtues. Sing, listen, and keep love in your heart: pain will leave, and peace will come home. Then a run of lines about the Guru's word. Through the Guru comes the sound, through the Guru the scripture, and through the Guru the One is everywhere. The Guru, it says, is Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma; the Guru is Parvati, the mother. Sikh commentators read this as saying that everything people honor in those great names is found in the Guru's word. Then Nanak says something disarmingly honest: even if I knew Him, I couldn't describe Him; there's no telling it. And then the refrain. Guraa ik dehi bujhaaee: O Guru, give me this one understanding. Sabhnaa jeeaa kaa ik daataa, so mai visar na jaaee: of all living beings there is one Giver; may I not forget Him. Visar is to forget, to let slip from the mind; na jaaee, may it not happen. That's the whole request. Not wealth, not answers to every question, not even the power to describe God. Just memory. If there is one Giver of everything, forgetting the Giver is the main thing that can go wrong. And remembering is simran, the practice from camp three, the thing Japji's title word, jap, asks for.
screen: `NOT INSTALLED, NOT MADE.` · `SING, LISTEN, KEEP LOVE.` · `ONE GIVER OF ALL BEINGS.` · `VISAR — TO LET SLIP.` · then, large: `MAY I NOT FORGET.`

Notice how many hands there are, and where they all begin. If you pray, you can thank the one Giver with a single word, Waheguru.

173.title: Pauri 6, sound: teerath naavaa
173.howItsDone: The sixth pauri of Japji is recited each morning; like the fifth, it ends with the refrain asking the Guru for one understanding, that there is one Giver of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, visar, to let slip from the mind, and the one Giver of pauri five. Your line was may I not forget.

At Haridwar on the Ganges, people step down the ghats at dawn into cold water. Other rivers and lakes draw people too, someone come to wash off a hard year. The janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak's life, say he walked to places like these. The sixth pauri of Japji opens on the riverbank, with a line about bathing, and its first line rings: two words that rhyme, side by side, like two feet stepping into water.
screen: `STEPS DOWN INTO A RIVER.` → `WASHING OFF A HARD YEAR.` → `TWO WORDS THAT RHYME.`

segments.voice: The opening line: teerath naavaa, je tis bhaavaa. Teerath: TEE-rath. A teerath is a pilgrimage place, a holy ford, a spot on a river where people bathe. Naavaa: NAA-vaa, I would bathe. Je: jay, if. Tis: tiss, to Him. Bhaavaa: BHAA-vaa, I were pleasing. I would bathe at the holy place, if I were pleasing to Him. Hear the rhyme: naavaa, bhaavaa, the two halves landing on the same sound, like an echo. Then the line goes on: vin bhaane ki naae karee. Vin: without. Bhaane: pleasing. Ki: what. Naae karee: bathing would I do. Without pleasing Him, what bathing would I do? That opens tomorrow. Today, the music. Guru Nanak builds this pauri from rhyme and repetition, easy to carry in your head. One line holds a string of treasures: ratan, javaahar, maanik, jewels, gems and rubies; you can hear their weight just in the sound. And the refrain from pauri five comes back: guraa ik dehi bujhaaee, O Guru, give me this one understanding. When a refrain repeats, it's telling you what to hold onto: two pauris in a row end on the same request.
screen: `TEERATH — A HOLY FORD.` · `NAAVAA, BHAAVAA — A RHYME.` · `RATAN, JAVAAHAR, MAANIK.` · `THE REFRAIN COMES BACK.` · then, large: `PAURI SIX.`

Then sit, picture cool water around your feet, and breathe; if you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

174.title: Pauri 6, meaning: jewels within
174.hook: pilgrimage bathing is worth it only if it pleases Him; the mind holds jewels when it hears the Guru's teaching (Japji 6)
174.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the sixth pauri each morning; its line about jewels in the mind is quoted in talks on why listening to Gurbani matters.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ratan, a jewel, and the sound of pauri six. Your line was teerath naavaa.

A man spends his whole life traveling the world looking for treasure, comes home poor, and then finds it buried under his own kitchen floor. People tell that old story in many cultures. So often the looking goes far away, for what's close. Guru Nanak's sixth pauri says something like it, standing on yesterday's riverbank. The jewels, it says, are closer than the river.

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. If I please Him, that is my pilgrimage bath; if I don't, what good is bathing? I look at the whole creation: without His grace, what does anyone receive? Then: mat vich ratan javaahar maanik, je ik gur kee sikh sunee. In the mind there are jewels, gems and rubies, if you listen to even one teaching of the Guru. Mat is the mind, the understanding. Ratan, javaahar, maanik: three words for precious stones, piled up so you feel the weight. The key is sikh, which here means a teaching, an instruction. The word Sikh itself is usually traced to the same root: a learner, one who receives the teaching. On that reading, a Sikh is someone who listens for the jewels. Notice what the pauri doesn't say. It doesn't mock anyone for bathing in a river; Guru Nanak stood at those rivers, the stories say, and people still come to them. It says the bath is only as good as the heart that steps into it, and that what really washes and enriches a person is inside, waiting to be heard. Then the refrain returns: O Guru, give me this one understanding, that there is one Giver of all beings; may I not forget Him. The jewels were never imported from somewhere else. They're what's left when one teaching is actually heard. One, not a library.
screen: `A BATH IS ONLY AS GOOD AS THE HEART.` · `MAT — THE MIND.` · `RATAN, JAVAAHAR, MAANIK.` · `SIKH — ONE WHO HEARS THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `JEWELS WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Look inward, as if opening a small box you haven't opened in a while, and find one jewel in yourself: not something you've achieved but something you are, like patience that shows up when it matters, a way of making people laugh, or the attention you give a friend in trouble. Hold it a moment and ask where it came from: who taught you, what line you once heard and kept. If you pray, you can thank the Giver with Waheguru.
Mat. The mind, the understanding: what holds jewels, gems and rubies, when it hears even one teaching of the Guru.
Your line: jewels within. A single line, taken in, can do it. That's day one hundred seventy-four.

175.title: Pauri 7, sound: je jug chaare
175.hook: je jug chaare aarjaa hor dasoonee hoe
175.howItsDone: The seventh pauri of Japji is recited each morning; its long opening line about living through the four ages is one of the most memorable in the hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mat, the mind, and the jewels of pauri six. Your line was jewels within.

If you could live as long as you wanted, how long would you choose? A hundred years? A thousand? People have always dreamed about it, from old legends of sages who lived for ages to today's headlines about slowing down aging. The seventh pauri of Japji opens with that dream and makes it enormous: a life as long as all four ages of the world, and then ten times more. It's a line about time, and it sounds like it's stretching.
screen: `HOW LONG WOULD YOU CHOOSE?` → `FOUR AGES OF THE WORLD.` → `THEN TEN TIMES MORE.`

segments.voice: The opening line: je jug chaare aarjaa, hor dasoonee hoe. Je: jay, if. Jug: like the English word jug, but shorter, closer to joog; it's an age, an era. You met it inside jugaad, through the ages. Chaare: CHAA-ray, all four; in Indian thought, time turns through four great ages, the four jugs. Aarjaa: AAR-jaa, a lifespan. Hor: and more. Dasoonee: da-SOO-nee, tenfold. Hoe: HO-ay, it were. If your lifespan were all four ages, and ten times more. The meaning, and a surprising twist, come tomorrow. Today, the sound. The line opens with short, quick words, je, jug, then gets longer: chaare, aarjaa, dasoonee. The syllables stretch, like the lifetime they describe. The next lines keep adding: nav khandaa vich jaaneeai, known in all nine regions of the world. Naal chalai sabh koe, with everyone walking along beside you. Changaa naau rakhaae kai, keeping a good name. Jas keerat jag lei, praise and fame in the world. Long life, fame, followers, reputation: a list getting bigger and bigger. And just when it's at its tallest, the pauri turns on a single short word: je. If. Hold on to that.
screen: `JUG — AN AGE. CHAARE — ALL FOUR.` · `AARJAA — A LIFESPAN.` · `THE LIST GETS BIGGER.` · `THEN ONE SHORT WORD: IF.` · then, large: `PAURI SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Say it slowly, out loud if you can, and let the long words stretch: je jug chaare aarjaa, hor dasoonee hoe. Say it twice more, the last time softly. Then sit and feel how long this one breath is, the only length of life you actually have in your hands right now; if you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.
